reference: The Godfather — the Louis Restaurant sit-down. Sal is Sollozzo, McClawsky is the bought cop, the Prospect is Michael. The gun is behind the cistern.
diagnosis: The flattest writing in the game. Every line is a summary of a feeling rather than a thing a person says. 'Business disagreement.' 'You hit me.' 'You were being difficult.' Nobody in a room where somebody is about to be shot in the face talks in four-word abstractions. The scene has no smell, no body, no money in it. Sal should be charming and obscene at once — he is asking a kid to sell his family and he does it like a man ordering veal. McClawsky is a cop on the take who despises everyone at the table including himself.

lines.why: Bellhop politeness from a bent cop. He is escorting a kid to a table where he expects him to fold; that should be in his mouth.
lines.house: Move, ape. He's been sat in there forty minutes with nothing in front of him but a glass of water and his own opinions.
lines.tarantino: Forty minutes he's been in that booth. No food, no paper, nothing to look at. You know what a man does with forty empty minutes? He starts deciding things. Let's get in there before he finishes.
lines.mcdonagh: Come on to fuck. He gets worse the longer he sits, and he started out fairly bad.
lines.houser: Let's go, big man. Table's under a name neither of us can spell, the meter's running, and I've got a wife who thinks I'm at a prayer group.
lines.coen: They're waiting on you. I don't like to be the one to say it. But they have been waiting a while now, and it's the kind of thing that gets noticed.

lines.current: The Sasquatches are making business difficult.
lines.why: A press release. Sal wants to sound reasonable, but 'difficult' costs him nothing to say and tells the player nothing about what he actually wants.
lines.house: Your family is costing me money in a way I can't put on a page. Every week I write a number down and every week your uncle makes it smaller with his hands.
lines.tarantino: You know what I like about your people? Commitment. Genuine, unreasonable commitment. I've got two docks, four routes, and a man in Tacoma who counts for me, and every one of them has been made stupid by sasquatches who will not take a phone call. That's not war. War I understand. That's just bad manners with a body count.
lines.mcdonagh: Your lot are ruinin' me. Not beatin' me, mind. Ruinin' me. There's a difference and it's mostly paperwork.
lines.houser: Let me be transparent with you, because I value transparency. Your family is a market inefficiency. You're sitting on distribution you don't understand, running it like a hobby, and I'm the one man in this city willing to professionalize it before somebody less friendly does it for free.
lines.coen: Things have been difficult. Business-wise. I don't want to overstate it. But I've had to have conversations I'd rather not have had, and I'd say that's on your family, more or less.

lines.why: Statement of fact with no injury in it. The kid watched his people get shot; this reads like a customer-service complaint.
lines.house: You put four in my uncle outside a fruit stand and now you want to talk about routes.
lines.tarantino: See, that's a nice word. Difficult. My uncle's got a bag on his side he has to empty himself, and you're sat there saying difficult like the traffic was bad.
lines.mcdonagh: You shot up my family, you're sat there orderin' veal, and you've the neck to call us difficult.
lines.houser: You sent men to my family's business with guns and now you're pitching me a partnership. Is there a brochure?
lines.coen: You shot my people. That's — I mean, that happened. That's a thing that happened and now we're eating.

lines.why: The single worst line in the scene. Two words of nothing where the audience needs to hear a man rationalize murder to a victim's face.
lines.house: Your uncle said no to me in front of people. There's no version of that where he stays standing.
lines.tarantino: It was a negotiation. Negotiations have positions. Your uncle took his position, I took mine, mine had more men in it. Don't confuse the outcome with the intent — I liked him.
lines.mcdonagh: It was business. He said no, and he said it loud, and there was a fella from Seattle watchin'. What was I meant to do, send a card?
lines.houser: That was a restructuring. Nobody enjoys a restructuring. But you don't take it personally, because the alternative is everybody gets restructured, including me.
lines.coen: Well. There was a disagreement. It got away from everybody a little. That's how these things tend to go, in my experience.

lines.why: Three words. No image, no weight. The player should make the room look at what was done.
lines.house: You shot Booski in the gut on a Tuesday and left him crawling to a payphone.
lines.tarantino: You shot Booski. In the stomach. Which — and I want you to hear this — is the one place you shoot a man when you want him to have time to think about it.
lines.mcdonagh: You shot Booski. In the stomach. Four times. He's forty-one and he shits in a bag now, so.
lines.houser: You shot Booski. He's got a colostomy bag and a lawsuit and neither one of them's covered.
lines.coen: You shot Booski. He's — he's not doing great, is the thing. It's not the kind of thing that heals up.

lines.why: Same problem — bloodless. Sal should sound almost hurt, which is what makes him frightening.
lines.house: Booski turned me down in a parking lot with his back to me. That's not a no, that's an insult with a witness.
lines.tarantino: Booski heard a very good offer, made a face, and walked away mid-sentence. Mid-sentence. Now I've got no problem with no. No is half of business. But you finish the sentence, and then you say it.
lines.mcdonagh: Booski said no. Fine. Grand. Then he laughed. And that's the bit that got him shot, if we're bein' precise about it, which we should be.
lines.houser: Booski declined a very generous package. No counter-offer, no conversation, just a hand in my face. And I'm a man who believes in consequences for bad negotiators.
lines.coen: He said no. Which is his right. But he said it in a way that — you know, there were people there. And then things went the way they went.

lines.current: Your people need to calm down.
lines.why: A hall monitor. This is a cop who takes Sal's money — he should be openly bought, openly contemptuous, and enjoying his own leverage.
lines.house: Your people need to sit down before I start finding things in their cars.
lines.tarantino: Here's my position, and I'm only in this booth because the food's free. Your people get loud, I get phone calls. I don't like phone calls. So either you take the man's money, or I start being the kind of police officer that ruins a whole family over a taillight.
lines.mcdonagh: Your lot need to calm the fuck down. I've a stack of unsolveds on my desk with your surname on 'em and a very flexible attitude to who did what.
lines.houser: Let me frame this from a law-enforcement perspective. Every one of your uncles is one traffic stop from a very long weekend, and I decide what's in the trunk when we open it.
lines.coen: Your people ought to settle down some. I'm saying that as a friend, more or less. It's not a threat. But it's not not a threat, either.

lines.why: Playground. The player is looking at the cop who broke his jaw and this is what comes out.
lines.house: You broke my jaw on a wet sidewalk while two of your guys held my arms.
lines.tarantino: You broke my jaw. Outside a hospital. With a flashlight. And then you got back in the car and finished your coffee, which is the part I keep coming back to.
lines.mcdonagh: You broke my jaw, you fat fuck. I've a plate in it. Sets off the machine at the airport.
lines.houser: You broke my jaw outside a hospital and then filed it as resisting. I've read the report. It's beautiful. You should write books.
lines.coen: You hit me. In the face. With a flashlight. I don't know that anybody's mentioned that yet tonight.

lines.why: Echoes Sal's word without meaning to; both men now sound like the same bland person. The cop's excuse should be uglier and funnier than the boss's.
lines.house: You were standing where I told you not to stand. Twice.
lines.tarantino: You were standing in a hospital corridor at two in the morning telling me about my job. In my experience, that's a conversation that ends the same way every time, and this time it ended with a flashlight.
lines.mcdonagh: You were in my way. And you'd a mouth on you. And I'd had a long day, so between the three of us, somethin' had to give.
lines.houser: You were obstructing an officer, and I want you to know I have four witnesses who'd swear to it under oath and one of them's a priest.
lines.coen: Well, you were being difficult. And I'd had a long shift. I'm not proud of it. But I'd do it again, is the honest truth.

lines.current: I want the servers, the skin market, and Wednesday nights.
lines.why: This one is actually close — the specificity is right. It just lands too clean; Sal should be greedier and more obscene about wanting it.
lines.house: I want the servers, the skin market, and every Wednesday night from now until the sun burns out.
lines.tarantino: Three things. The servers. The skin market. And Wednesdays. That's it. That's the whole list. I'm not asking for the jerky — I don't want the jerky, the jerky is a nightmare, God bless whoever handles the jerky.
lines.mcdonagh: The servers, the skins, and Wednesdays. And before you say it — no, I don't want the jerky. I've seen where it comes from.
lines.houser: I want the servers, the skin market, and Wednesday nights. That's infrastructure, retail, and footfall. Everything else you can keep, including the meat, which I want on record I have never eaten.
lines.coen: I'd want the servers. The skin market. And the Wednesdays. That's — that's the ask. I've written it down if you want to see it written down.

lines.why: Ceremonial. Reads like a motto on a crest instead of a kid defending the one night that pays for everything.
lines.house: Wednesday pays for everything. Wednesday is why my aunt has a house.
lines.tarantino: Wednesday's not a night. Wednesday's the whole thing. Wednesday is why there's a roof on my aunt's place and why nobody in my family has ever had a real job. You're not asking for a night, you're asking for the last forty years.
lines.mcdonagh: Wednesday's ours. Wednesday's been ours since before you'd a second shoe.
lines.houser: Wednesday isn't a night, it's a revenue stream, and you know it, which is why you put it last like it was an afterthought.
lines.coen: Wednesdays are the family's. That's — that's been the case a long time. Longer than you've been around, and I mean that respectfully.

lines.current: Everything belongs to someone until it changes hands.
lines.why: Fortune cookie. It is trying to be the scene's cold thesis line and instead sounds like a magnet on a fridge.
lines.house: Everything belongs to somebody right up until somebody stronger wants it. That's not philosophy, kid, that's just Tuesday.
lines.tarantino: Belongs. That's a beautiful word. My father used it about a farm in Calabria that has had six owners since he said it. Things don't belong to people. Things sit with people, for a while, until somebody with more men wants them to sit somewhere else.
lines.mcdonagh: Everything belongs to somebody. And then it doesn't. That's the whole of history, that is, and I've not even finished me drink.
lines.houser: Ownership is a story people agree to tell. And I'm here to tell you the room has stopped agreeing.
lines.coen: Well. Things belong to folks until they don't. That's about the size of it. I didn't make the rule.

lines.current: Help me, Prospect. The Sasquatches keep their territory. I get a percentage.
lines.why: The actual pitch, and it has no seduction in it. Sal is asking a kid to betray his father's house; he should make it sound like mercy.
lines.house: Help me, kid. Your family keeps the name, keeps the corners, keeps the funerals small. I take a slice off the top and nobody has to bury anybody they like.
lines.tarantino: Here's what I'm actually offering you, and I want you to hear it without your uncle's voice in your ear. Your family keeps everything. The name, the territory, the whole ugly circus. I take a percentage off the top and in exchange, nobody else in your family has to learn what a colostomy bag is. That's not a threat. That's the single most generous thing anybody has said to you this year.
lines.mcdonagh: Help me out, son. Your lot keep the lot. I take a cut. And the shootin' stops, which I'd have thought was the headline, but nobody ever leads with it.
lines.houser: I'm offering you a licensing arrangement. You retain the brand, the territory, and all the charming regional character. I take a percentage and provide what I'd call stability, which in your industry means your mother doesn't get a phone call.
lines.coen: Help me out here. You folks keep your territory. I take a percentage. Everybody goes home. It's not complicated, and I'd hate for it to become complicated.

lines.why: Fine as a beat but too small a hook for the reply it sets up; the kid can put a little teeth on it.
lines.house: How big a slice are we calling a percentage?
lines.tarantino: Percentage. Okay. See, a percentage is a number. So say the number.
lines.mcdonagh: What percentage? And don't say 'a fair one,' I'll lose me mind.
lines.houser: Define percentage. Because in my experience that word does a lot of heavy lifting for men with your job.
lines.coen: What percentage would that be? Just — ballpark. For my own information.

lines.why: The one word here that already works. Keep it; the variants only change the temperature.
lines.house: Enough.
lines.tarantino: Enough that you'll notice. Not so much you'd die over it. I've done the math on that particular line more times than you've been alive.
lines.mcdonagh: Enough. Next question.
lines.houser: A meaningful one. I'll have my accountant walk you through it, and you'll hate him, everybody does.
lines.coen: Enough. I'd rather not put a number on it at the table.

lines.current: I need to use the bathroom.
lines.why: Functional, and it telegraphs the mechanic. The Godfather beat works because the excuse is so ordinary it embarrasses the room. Give it a body.
lines.house: I gotta piss.
lines.tarantino: I need the bathroom. It's the jaw — they've got me on something for it and it goes straight through me. Two minutes.
lines.mcdonagh: I need a piss. Sorry. It's the pills for me face, they run through you somethin' shockin'.
lines.houser: I need the men's room. And before either of you says anything clever about it — yes, it's the nerves, and yes, I'd rather go now than on your upholstery.
lines.coen: I need to use the restroom. I'm sorry. It's been a lot of coffee and, you know, a lot of everything.

lines.why: Right idea, no relish. The cop is bragging about his own thoroughness one minute before it kills him — that irony should be audible.
lines.house: Go on. I checked it myself. Tank, towels, the little window. Wash your hands.
lines.tarantino: Go ahead. I checked it before you got here — cistern, towel dispenser, that little window nobody fits through. There's nothing in there but a bar of soap and your own reflection, and I'd say the soap's the friendlier of the two.
lines.mcdonagh: Off you go. I checked it meself. Twice. I'm very thorough, that's me whole personality.
lines.houser: Be my guest. I swept it personally — that's twenty-two years of policing applied to a toilet, and I want you to appreciate what that cost the taxpayer.
lines.coen: Sure, go ahead. We had a look in there already. Nothing to it. Wash your hands, though. That's just — that's just good practice.

lines.why: Serviceable but generic. It is the last order he ever gives; make it his.
lines.house: Sit your ass down, Squatch.
lines.tarantino: Sit down. You're the tallest thing in the room and it's making the waiter nervous.
lines.mcdonagh: Sit down, would you. You're loomin'. I hate loomin'.
lines.houser: Sit. You're standing like a man with a plan and it's ruining my appetizer.
lines.coen: Why don't you sit down. You're making everybody look up, and that's — nobody enjoys that.

lines.why: Two syllables of nothing at the tensest moment in the scene — the gun is not where it should be. This is where the player's panic lives.
lines.house: Come on. Come on, it's supposed to be right here.
lines.tarantino: It's supposed to be here. Behind the tank, taped, he said behind the tank. So either I'm looking at the wrong tank or somebody's about to find out how fast I can run.
lines.mcdonagh: Where is it. Where is it. He said behind the jacks. He said it twice. I'll kill him. If I live, I'll kill him.
lines.houser: It's not here. It's not here. Fantastic. Everybody in this organization can shoot a man in a fruit stand but nobody can tape a pistol to a toilet.
lines.coen: It's supposed to be here. He said it'd be here. That's what he said, and now it isn't, and I've got about forty seconds.

lines.why: Fine as a nudge; variants add the specific menace of a man who has noticed something.
lines.house: Prospect.
lines.tarantino: Kid. You went somewhere just then. Come back.
lines.mcdonagh: Are you with us? You've gone very still, and I don't like still.
lines.houser: You've drifted. And in my experience, when a young man drifts at a table like this, he's either scared or he's counting, and I'd like to know which.
lines.coen: Son? You still with us here?

lines.why: Same note twice. Escalate instead of repeating.
lines.house: Look at me when I'm buying your family.
lines.tarantino: Because I'd hate to be doing this twice. I'm not a man who enjoys saying a thing twice — ask anybody who used to work for me.
lines.mcdonagh: Am I talkin' to meself here? I might as well be talkin' to the fuckin' napkin.
lines.houser: I'm going to need engagement. This is the biggest conversation of your life and you're looking at the salt.
lines.coen: Are you hearing me? Because I've said it now and I'd rather not have said it for nothing.

lines.current: So. Do we have an understanding?
lines.why: Close to right, but it is the beat before the killing and it should feel like a hand being offered over a table with blood already on it.
lines.house: So. Do we have an understanding, or do I finish my drink and make some calls?
lines.tarantino: So. Understanding. That's the word we're using. Do we have one, or do I finish this and go make three phone calls I'd genuinely rather not make?
lines.mcdonagh: So. Are we grand, or are we not grand? Because I've a table booked elsewhere at ten and one way or the other I'm makin' it.
lines.houser: So. Are we aligned? And I want a yes or a no, not one of those beautiful family answers where nobody's said anything.
lines.coen: So. Do we have an understanding here? Because I'd like to think we do. I'd like to go home thinking we do.

lines.why: It is meant to be the lie the kid tells with a gun already in his belt. As written there is nothing under it.
lines.house: We understand each other.
lines.tarantino: I understand you completely. That's the first true thing anybody's said at this table.
lines.mcdonagh: I understand you. I do. I understand you perfectly.
lines.houser: I understand. I understand exactly what's on offer and exactly what it costs.
lines.coen: I understand. Yeah. I think I've got the shape of it now.

lines.current: Good. The Sasquatches keep their name.
lines.why: Reads as a concession being read from a list. Sal should sound generous, warm, almost fond — the last thing he ever feels.
lines.house: Good. Your family keeps the name. That's worth more than the money and your uncle's too proud to admit it.
lines.tarantino: Good. You keep the name. And don't underrate that — the name's the only thing in this business nobody can take off you with a car and four men.
lines.mcdonagh: Good man. You keep the name. Everyone loves a name. Sure the name's half the fun of it.
lines.houser: Excellent. You retain the name, the heritage, the whole beautiful folk mythology. I'm not a barbarian, I'm a partner.
lines.coen: Good. Good. You keep the name. That's important to folks, and I respect that. I do.

lines.why: The cop's last line in his life, and it is a greeting card. It should be smug, venal, and a little too pleased with itself.
lines.house: And everybody walks out of here with all their teeth. Which is more than I usually manage on a Thursday.
lines.tarantino: And everybody walks away happy. Which is rare. In twenty-two years I have been at maybe four tables where everybody walked away happy, and two of those I was lying.
lines.mcdonagh: And everyone goes home happy. Well. Happy-ish. Happy enough, which is the most anyone gets.
lines.houser: And everybody walks away happy, and I get to expense the veal. This is what community policing looks like.
lines.coen: And everybody walks away happy. That's the goal. That's always been the goal, whatever anybody says about me.

lines.current: Tell your people the business is settled.
lines.why: Correct content, no music. This is the cue the player kills him on; it wants a last beat of warmth so the violence lands.
lines.house: Go tell your people it's settled. Tell your uncle I asked after him.
lines.tarantino: Go home. Tell your people it's settled. And tell your uncle — tell him Sal asked after him. He'll make a face. Let him make the face.
lines.mcdonagh: Tell your lot it's sorted. And tell your uncle I was askin' for him. He'll not like that, which is why I'm sayin' it.
lines.houser: Take the good news home. Tell them it's settled, tell them it was amicable, and tell your uncle his health is very much on my mind.
lines.coen: You go on and tell your people it's settled. And — you know. Give my best to your uncle. Sincerely.

lines.why: The trigger line. Two words is right, but 'It is' is limp. It needs to be the last thing Sal hears and sound like a door closing.
lines.house: It's settled.
lines.tarantino: Yeah. It's settled.
lines.mcdonagh: It's sorted.
lines.houser: Consider it settled.
lines.coen: It's settled. Yeah.
